questions.question: A merchant marks the price of his article 20 percent above the cost price. He gives some discount on it and earns a profit of 10 percent. What is the discount percentage?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Ratio of **Cost Price (CP)** to **Marked Price (MP)** = 100 : 120 = 5 : 6.

Ratio of **Cost Price (CP)** to **Selling Price (SP)** = 100 : 110 = 10 : 11.

By equating **CP** (multiply first ratio by 2): **CP** = 10, **MP** = 12, **SP** = 11.

**Discount %** = (Difference between MP and SP ÷ MP) × 100.

**Discount %** = (12 − 11) ÷ 12 × 100 = 100 ÷ 12 = 8.33%.

**∴ The correct answer is 8.33 percent.**

**__Alternate Method__**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/a2fed9bf624998b07584c95e284f460263f8d2eed753c818bcdd2f64ebcb8ffc.png] 

⇒ Let the **Cost Price (CP)** of the article be 100.

⇒ **Marked Price (MP)** = **CP** + 20% of **CP** = 100 + 20 = 120.

⇒ **Profit Percentage** = 10%.

⇒ **Selling Price (SP)** = **CP** + 10% of **CP** = 100 + 10 = 110.

⇒ **Discount Amount** = **MP** − **SP** = 120 − 110 = 10.

⇒ **Discount Percentage** = (**Discount** ÷ **MP**) × 100.

⇒ **Discount %** = (10 ÷ 120) × 100 = 8.33%.

**∴ The correct answer is 8.33 percent.**

**__Additional Information__**

Direct Relation Formula

The relation between **CP**, **MP**, **Profit %** (P), and **Discount %** (D) is given by: **MP / CP = (100 + P) / (100 − D)**.

Successive Percentage Change

The net profit can be calculated using the formula: **Net Profit% = M − D − (M × D) / 100**, where M is Markup % and D is Discount %.

Marked Price and Selling Price

**Marked Price** is also known as the **List Price**. **Selling Price** is always **MP − Discount** or **CP + Profit**.</p

For a path of **width (w)** built **outside** a **rectangular garden** of **length (L)** and **breadth (B)**:

Path Inside the Garden

Cross Paths

Circular Path

questions.question: A boat travels in upstream from point P to Q for 6 hours and while returning travels in downstream from point Q to R for next 6 hours. If the distance between points P and R is 72 km, then what is the speed of the stream?
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

In equal time intervals (T), the difference between Downstream distance and Upstream distance is 2 × stream speed (v) × time (T).

Difference in distances (PR) = 72 km

Time (T) = 6 hours

Formula: 2 × v × T = Distance Difference

2 × v × 6 = 72 ⇒ 12v = 72

v = 72 ÷ 12 = 6 km/hr

**∴ The correct answer is 6 km/hr.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Time for Upstream (P to Q) = 6 hours

Time for Downstream (Q to R) = 6 hours

Distance PR = 72 km

**Formula Used:**

Speed = Distance ÷ Time

Upstream Speed (Sᵤ) = u − v

Downstream Speed (Sd) = u + v

where u = speed of boat in still water and v = speed of stream.

 
 
•

**Calculations:**

⇒ Distance PQ = Upstream speed × Time = (u − v) × 6

⇒ Distance QR = Downstream speed × Time = (u + v) × 6

⇒ As R is the downstream destination from Q, and P is the upstream start for Q, the distance PR = QR − PQ.

⇒ 72 = 6(u + v) − 6(u − v)

⇒ 72 = 6u + 6v − 6u + 6v

⇒ 72 = 12v

⇒ v = 72 ÷ 12

⇒ v = 6 km/hr

**∴ The correct answer is 6 km/hr.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Downstream and Upstream Speed

Downstream Speed (Sd) = u + v and Upstream Speed (Sᵤ) = u − v, where u is boat speed and v is stream speed.

Speed of Boat in Still Water

It is calculated as the average of downstream and upstream speeds: u = (Sd + Sᵤ) ÷ 2.

Speed of the Stream

It is half the difference between downstream and upstream speeds: v = (Sd − Sᵤ) ÷ 2.

questions.question: Which of the following is a complex permanent plant tissue?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Xylem**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Complex Permanent Tissue: A **cluster of structurally distinct cells** carrying out a common function or series of functions is referred to as complex permanent tissue. They are **composed of various cell types**. 
 
• Phloem and xylem are **examples** of these tissues. 
 
 
• Xylem:
 
 
• It facilitates the movement of water and dissolved materials throughout the plant.
 
• The various parts of the xylem consist of **parenchyma**, vessels, tracheids, and xylem fibers.
 
• **Lignin **makes up the xylem fibers and **cheids**, which give the plant structural support.
 
 
 
• Phloem:
 
 
• Food particles can be transported with the help of phloem.
 
• Complementary cells, sieve cells, sieve tubes, phloem fibers, and phloem parenchyma make up phloem.
 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Permanent tissues: Although these cells can no longer spread, they are specialized to provide the plant with strength, elasticity, and flexibility.

 
 
• These tissues also fall into the following categories:
 
 
• Simple Permanent Tissue
 
• Complex Permanent Tissue​​
 
 
 
 
 
• Collenchyma: These are live, **elongated cells** with minuscule spaces between them.
 
 
• **Pectin **and **cellulose **make up their cell walls.
 
• It provides plants with mechanical support and a flexible structural framework.
 
• It is **found on the margins of leaves** and **stems**.
 
 
 
• Plants have an **apical meristem**, an area of cells that can divide and **expand at the terminals of their roots and shoots**.
 
 
• The apical meristems extend the roots and shoots and **give rise to the main body of the plant**.
 
• Because this and other meristems can divide indefinitely, unlike most mammals, plants can grow for the entirety of their lives.
 
 
 
• **Lateral meristems** : This kind of meristem is found along the stem and root's longitudinal axis.
 
 
• Another name for it is a **secondary meristem.**
 
• Through division, the lateral meristem's cells proliferate and aid in the **thickening of the stem and root**.
 
• One kind of lateral meristem that creates the xylem and phloem is the **vascular cambium**.

questions.question: Which state government has introduced India's first elephant death audit framework?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tamil Nadu**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Tamil Nadu **has launched the "**Tamil Nadu Elephant Death Audit Framework**," a **first-of-its-kind project in India**, to better account for elephant fatalities by documenting their causes.
 
• At the State Wildlife Board meeting, **Chief Minister MK Stalin** made this announcement.
 
• The framework aims to achieve **three key goals**:
 
 
• firstly, it provides a systematic standard protocol for conducting post-mortems to identify the cause(s) of elephant deaths;
 
• secondly, it investigates and analyzes the circumstances surrounding elephant deaths that could have been prevented; and
 
• thirdly, it develops corrective measures to prevent unnatural and preventive deaths by conducting periodic death audits and tracking these over time.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Elephants in India**: According to **Project Elephant's 2017 census**, India is home to an **estimated 29,964 wild Asian elephants**, making it the **country with the highest population.**

 
 
• Approximately **60% of the species' global population** consists of it.
 
• **Karnataka **has the **highest number of elephants**, followed by Assam and Kerala.
 
 
 
• The **Indian Wild Life Protection Act of 1972** designates elephants as National Heritage animals and provides them with protection under the **Schedule** **I species.**
 
 
• With the primary goal of restoring elephant habitats and mitigating the suffering of elephants and the human population, the Indian government initiated "**Project Elephant" in 1991–1992**, a **Ministry of Environment, Forests & Climate Change** centrally sponsored scheme.
 
• Its goals included addressing the issue of human-animal conflict and offering financial and technical support to the Indian states that make up the elephant range in order to **safeguard the elephants**, their habitats, and their corridors.
 
• It also aimed to advance the welfare of elephants kept in captivity.
 
• The following** goals guided** the** launch of Project Elephant** (PE): 
 
 
• To protect elephants, their habitat & corridors
 
• To address issues of man-animal conflict
 
• Welfare of captive elephants

questions.question: Which country introduced the game of cricket?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**England**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The earliest documented mention of **cricket **is from the middle of the **16th century,** and it comes from **South East England**.
 
• With the first international matches played in the second half of the 19th century, it spread throughout the world along with the British Empire's expansion.
 
• In cricket,** two teams of eleven players** compete in a **bat-and-ball match** on a field that has a** 22-yard (20-meter) pitch** in the middle.
 
• Each team's wicket is made up of two bails balanced on three stumps.
 
• One member of the fielding team, the **bowler**, bowls the ball towards the striker's wicket from the other end of the pitch while two members of the **batting **team, the striker and nonstriker, stand in front of either wicket.
 
• In order for the batting team to score one run for each exchange, the striker's objective is to hit the bowled ball and then trade places with the nonstriker. Additionally, runs are counted when the ball is bowled or reaches or crosses the field's boundary.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **A**** **glossary of cricket terms:

 
 

 Terms
 Explanation
 
 

 Leg-Before Wicket (LBW)
 It's a way to get the batter out. In other words, the hitter is out if the umpire determines that the ball struck any portion of the batter's body—typically the leg—prior to striking the bat or missing the bat and would have struck the stumps.
 
 

 Maiden
 An over where no runs that are attributable to the bowler are scored (byes or leg-byes may be scored in this over, though, as these don't count against the bowler).
 
 

 Wide Ball
 A delivery that pitches too far away from the batsman and so proves impossible to score off. The umpire will single this by stretching his arms out horizontally; an extra will be added to the total and the ball will be bowled again.
 
 

 Bouncer
 A short-pitched ball which passes the batsman at chest or head height
 
 

 Chinaman
 A ball bowled by a left-arm slow bowler that turns into the right-hand batsman, in effect a left-arm legspinner. Named after Puss Achong.
 
 

 Mankad
 A term popular mainly in indoor cricket - but also fairly popular in Australia for outdoor cricket. Mankad is when the bowler brings his arm around and, instead of releasing the ball, runs out the non-striker by whipping off the bails. This type of dismissal is rare - and usually a warning is given to the batsman beforehand. Named after Vinod Mankad, who twice dismissed Australian Bill Brown this way.
 
 

 Doosra
 A Hindi/Urdu word which means "second" or "other", the doosra is the offspinner's version of the googly, delivered out of the back of the hand and turning away from the right-hand batsman.

questions.question: Who among the following led the Chittagong Armoury Raid?
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The** Chittagong Uprising**, also known as the **Chittagong Armoury Raid** by the British, was an attempt on **April 18, 1930**, by armed Indian independence activists** led by Surya Sen** to seize the police and auxiliary forces' armory from the Chittagong armoury in Bengal Province in British India (now in Bangladesh).
 
• The raiders belonged to the revolutionary** Indian Republican Army**, a group that supported armed rebellions as a way to free India from British colonial control.
 
• The group included **Ganesh Ghosh**, **Lokenath Bal**, **Ambika Chakrobarty**, **Harigopal Bal (Tegra)**, **Ananta Singh**, **Anand Prasad Gupta** etc.
 
• **Surya Sen**'s nickname, **Master Da**, came from his work as a **school teacher** .
 
 
• In 1916, while pursuing his B.A. at **Berhampore College (now MES College)**, he was impacted by nationalist ideas.
 
• He was chosen to **lead the Chittagong branch of the Indian National Congress in 1918.**
 
• He actively participated in the Non-Cooperation movement before being detained and held captive for two years, from 1926 to 1928, due to his revolutionary actions.
 
• Sen, a visionary and ebullient organizer, often quipped, "**Humanism is a special virtue of a revolutionary**."
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• ​​​Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel

 
 
• He was an Indian politician who held the positions of first Deputy Prime Minister and first Home Minister
 
• In addition to being an active member of the Indian National Congress, he practiced law. His birthdate was never officially documented. However, according to his matriculation exam documents, he was born on October 31, 1875.
 
• He was born in Gujarat, in Nadiad. Jhaverbhai Patel was his father, and Ladba was his mother. Siblings of Vallabhbhai Patel numbered five.
 
• He was often called Sardar.
 
• He was also called an Indian Bismarck.
 
• He was appointed as the President of the Indian National Congress during the Karachi session in 1931 
 
 
 
• Rabindranath Tagore:
 
 
• Bengali polymath Rabindranath Tagore (7 May 1861 – 7 August 1941) was involved in the Bengal Renaissance.
 
• He was a poet, novelist, playwright, composer, philosopher, social reformer, educator, and painter.
 
• Using Contextual Modernism in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, he transformed Indian art and music as well as Bengali literature.
 
• In 1913, he became the first non-European and the first lyricist to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
 
• He was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature in recognition of his work Geetanjali.
 
• In the 1915, King George V bestowed upon Tagore a knighthood, which he later renounced following the 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
 
• While Tagore's graceful prose and enchanted poetry were immensely well-liked throughout the Indian subcontinent, his poetic songs were perceived as mystical and mercurial.
 
• He was a fellow of the Royal Asiatic Society.
 
• Tagore was referred as "the Bard of Bengal" and went by the monikers Gurudeb, Kobiguru, and Biswokobi.
 
• Geetanjali, Sadhana, Ghare-Baire, Gora and Rabindra Sangeet are among his important works.
 
• His works, "Jana Gana Mana" in India and "Amar Shonar Bangla" in Bangladesh, were selected as national anthems by two countries. West Bengal has made "Banglar Mati Banglar Jol" into its official state anthem.
 
• In 1901 he founded the famous Shantiniketan which later came to be known as Vishwabharati University.
 
 
 
• **Vinayak Damodar Savarkar:**
 
 
• **​**He is also known as** ****Veer Savarkar**.
 
• He was born on **28th May,1883 **in **Bhagur**, a village near **Nashik **in Maharashtra.
 
• He founded a secret society called **Abhinav Bharat Society**.
 
• He went to the United Kingdom and was involved with organizations such as **India House** and the **Free India Society**.
 
• He was the **president **of **Hindu Mahasabha** from **1937 to 1943**.
 
• Savarkar wrote a **book **titled ‘**The History of the War of Indian Independence**’ in which he wrote **about **the guerilla warfare tricks used in **1857 Sepoy Mutiny**.
 
• He also wrote the **book **‘**Hindutva: who is hindu?**’.
 
• He was **arrested **in **1909 **on charges of plotting an armed revolt against the **Morley-Minto reform (Indian Councils Act 1909)** and was convicted and sentenced to **50-years imprisonment** also known as** Kala Pani **and** transported in 1911 to the Cellular Jail in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands**.

questions.question: __________ is the minimum amount of funds that the banks have to keep with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) as deposits.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Cash Reserve Ratio**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• 
 
Cash reserve ratio (CRR): 

 
 
• It is **a monetary policy tool **used **by** central banks including the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**, to **regulate **and control the **money supply** in the economy.
 
• **CRR **is the **percentage of total deposits that commercial banks are required to keep as reserves with the central bank**.
 
• It is a portion of the bank's demand and time liabilities.
 
• The **primary objective **of implementing CRR is to **ensure the liquidity and stability of the banking system **while controlling inflation and managing credit growth.
 
• When the **central bank** **increases the CRR**, it **reduces the amount of money available for lending by commercial banks**.
 
 
• This helps reduce excess liquidity in the economy, controlling inflationary pressures, and curbing excessive credit expansion.
 
 
 
• On the other hand, when the central bank decreases the CRR, it increases the amount of money available for lending by commercial banks.
 
• This can stimulate credit growth, promote economic activity, and ease liquidity conditions in the economy.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Repo Rate:

 
 
• It is the rate at which a nation's central bank lends money to commercial banks when there is a lack of funds by buying securities.
 
• In order to manage inflation, monetary authorities use repo rate.
 
• Central banks raise the repo rate in an effort to combat inflation since it discourages banks from borrowing.
 
• This eventually lowers the amount of money in circulation, which aids in containing inflation.
 
 
 
• 
 
Bank Rate:

 
 
• It is the rate at which commercial banks borrow money from the RBI without securities.
 
• The Reserve Bank of India regulates bank rates.
 
• Since it can control liquidity, it is typically higher than a repo rate.
 
 
 
• **​Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) :**
 
 
• It is a mechanism **used by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) **and other central banks to **implement monetary policy**.
 
• It **permits banks to lend money to the RBI through reverse repo agreements** or to receive money through repurchase agreements (repos).
 
• The **management of liquidity demands** and the **maintenance of fundamental market stability** are effectively achieved by this structure.
 
 
• Under its **open market operations**, the Federal Reserve of the United States transacts repos and reverse repos.
 
 
 
• The RBI **introduced **the LAF as a result of the **Narasimham Committee on Banking Sector Reforms (1998)**.
 
 
 
• 
 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is India’s central bank.

 
 
• In compliance with the terms of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, it was founded on April 1, 1935 in Calcutta.

 
 
• It was permanently moved to Mumbai in 1937.
 
 
 
• Though originally privately owned, since nationalisation in 1949, the Reserve Bank is fully owned by the Government of India.
 
• As a qualitative instrument of monetary policy, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) employs moral suasion.
 
• It regulates the issue of Bank notes and keeping of reserves with a view to securing monetary stability in India and generally to operate the currency and credit system of the country to its advantage.
 
• It also monitors the monetary policies through its Monetary Policy Committee (MPC).
